subject: axolotl
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: axolotl with frilly pink gills.
Style: chibi.
reasoning:
I'm planning out the chibi-style axolotl design with the SDK, thinking through proportions like a big head, stubby limbs, a finned tail, and frilly gill stalks, plus pink coloring to capture a cute, simplified look.

Now I'm working through the skeleton structure—placing root hips joint, spine chain from hips forward to chest/neck/head, and a tail chain extending backward—following a bone-sweep approach to build the body shape along the path.

For the head, I'm sizing it wide and flat to match the axolotl's chibi look, using a scaled sphere for the skull and a separate jaw bone with a flattened sphere for the lower jaw, colored a paler pink, plus a dark curved seam to suggest the signature wide mouth line.

Draping where jaw meets skull risks weird jumps at the seam, so maybe a decal approach is safer—an SVG-style smile and eyes texture directly on the skull surface. For a chibi look, big shiny eyes could work better as actual spherical parts rather than decals, so I'm weighing that tradeoff.

Placing the eye decals on the top-front of the head at symmetric azimuth angles using surface normals, and projecting a wide smile decal centered lower on the front of the skull.

I'm reconsidering the jaw structure—thinking it should be a separate flattened ellipsoid positioned below and forward of the skull, so it can hinge open independently while the mouth decal stays anchored to the skull itself.

I'm second-guessing how to visually separate the skull and jaw at their seam—maybe skip a mouth decal entirely and just rely on the pink skull versus pale jaw coloring to suggest the transition, rather than trying to place a precise smile line. I think it's cleaner to just construct the head as two explicit pieces rather than fuss over the exact seam geometry.

Writing lathe geometry logic...

Below that I'm adding the lower jaw as a half-ellipsoid hinged at the back, with the flat seam at the mouth opening colored dark rose to read as the interior, plus a tongue detail inside.

For the smile, I'm planning a curved line along the front half of that seam ellipse, with the corners sweeping upward at the cheeks to give that classic axolotl grin shape.

I'm working out a helper function that maps angle and height to a point on the dome surface, scaling the radius so the curve hugs the skull properly. Then I'm planning the cheeks as pink blush ovals and placing big round chibi eyes on the front-lateral sides of the dome, axolotl-style.

Now I'm figuring out exact placement coordinates for the eyes near the dome's upper sides, and setting up a surface-decal system that positions textures using azimuth and elevation angles on the lathe-based skull mesh. I'm sketching the eye texture itself as a big black shape with two white highlights for a glint, kept symmetric without needing mirroring.

Writing decal parameters...

Skipping the eyelid detail for simplicity, with a small white spec decal baked into the texture. Now I'm thinking through the gills as a signature feature—three curved stalks per side sweeping back and up from the head, each lined with many thin filament cards, built as a joint chain so they can fan out from a spread resting pose.

I'm working out how to construct each gill as a chain-and-sweep combo, sprouting from the head surface with the chain's root joint parented to the head, positioning them at roughly ±115° azimuth on the back-sides of the head so they angle mostly laterally.

Now I'm defining specific base-and-tip coordinates for three stalks per side (top, mid, low), each curving outward, backward, and slightly upward or downward depending on height.

I need to make sure no geometry dips below the floor, keeping the lowest stalk's tip lifted to around y=0.06, and planning to attach feathery pink filament cards along each stalk using a textured SVG asset.

For generating the filament placement, I'm working out how to sample points along the stalk sweep at multiple clock angles so filaments radiate outward on both sides rather than just one, orienting each card frame to face outward along the surface normal.

I'll allow some loose typing here since strict correctness matters less than getting the visual right, using the per-frame tangent as the flow direction so filaments lean naturally along the curving stalk. For the card texture, I'm picturing a thin tapered pink strand like a feather frond, roughly 0.03 wide and 0.055 long, double-sided and oriented along that flow direction.

But thinking it through, if flow equals the stalk tangent, the card's normal ends up pointing along the stalk too, which means viewed from the side the cards go edge-on and nearly disappear -- not what I want. I need the frond to lie flat in the plane formed by the stalk's tangent and its outward normal, so it reads as a broad leaning feather rather than a sliver.

That edge-on problem makes me reconsider: with flow along tangent, the card only reads face-on from one viewing direction, which isn't enough. So I'm trying a crossed-card approach instead—two perpendicular cards through each spine so at least one is readable from any angle, with lean tilting the card toward the tangent within the plane containing axis and flow, and width running perpendicular to that lean.

I'm estimating total card count across stalks and positions, then working out the angular distribution around each stalk—trying a few options like four cardinal angles or alternating offsets to make the fronds look feathery from all sides rather than flat.

I'm also planning the color treatment: a deeper pink-red at the stalk base fading to lighter pink at the filament tips, likely baked into the texture gradient rather than handled via vertex tinting.

Still writing texture shape code...

For the body coloring, I'm going for a leucistic pink axolotl look: light pink base, paler belly, slightly deeper dorsal tone with subtle darker speckles using a countershade and spot combination, plus warm-on-top cool-below lighting to give it form.

Writing the custom skin paint function...

Now I'm thinking through the skeleton layout — floor at y=0, an elongated plump body for the chibi axolotl with a flattened tail fin, trying to nail the proportions.

I'm placing the hip joint and a spine chain of points curving from hips to neck, then figuring out where the head pivot should sit relative to the back of the skull.

Checking total body length against a real axolotl's proportions, I realize my current measurements add up to roughly 0.51m, way bigger than intended. I'll scale everything down to keep the overall length closer to 0.3m, though I'm debating whether to apply a global scale factor or just redesign the numbers directly.

Actually, scaling everything with a helper function feels error-prone since I'd need to remember to apply it consistently to decals and geometry alike. It's simpler to just design directly in final meters from the start, so I'm setting up constants like floor level, body axis height, and the head's mouth plane and center position.

I'm working out the skull dome and jaw dimensions, placing the head roughly 0.12 wide and 0.124 long, then sizing the body and tail behind it—aiming for a shorter, chibi-style tail since a full 0.337m total length feels too long compared to a real axolotl's 0.25m. Trimming the tail brings the total down to about 0.307m, and now I'm placing the hip joint position.

Now I'm laying out the spine chain as a sequence of points running from the hips forward to around the shoulders, using a catmull spline through four points to create three joint spans named spine1 through spine3. I'm debating whether the hips joint should just be the root with a "spine" role, or whether it needs to be a separate joint from the first spine chain point, since they'd otherwise overlap in position.

I'm placing the head joint forward from the spine with a slight upward offset, then adding a jaw joint hinged at the head for mouth movement. For the body shape, I'm planning a smooth curve running from the tail tip through the hips up to the chest to define the overall silhouette.

Splitting that curve at the hips, I'm building separate spine and tail chains outward in each direction, both parented to the hips joint, then sweeping a radius profile along the whole path using all three bones together to form the full body mesh.

With count 5 giving 5 joints and matching names, I'm assigning the spine and tail roles, then laying out the body path points from tail tip to chest with y-values rising slightly, tapering the radii as the tail thins toward a membrane fin.

Mapping radii along the path as a function of normalized position, I'm defining key tail/hip/body widths and heights at several t-values, planning a helper function to interpolate between these radius pairs smoothly.

Now I'm checking the floor contact constraint: computing body center heights and ry values at the hip region and later points to confirm the lowest body edges stay within the allowed 2% sink tolerance into the floor.

I should bump up the sweep sides to around 12 for a rounder, smoother body rather than a faceted low-poly look. Checking the head dimensions, I need to make sure the dome's bottom plane doesn't awkwardly overlap with the body's top radius given the chest size.

Actually I realize the body is poking through the top of the head dome — the body top ends up taller than the head dome's top, which breaks the chibi proportions where the head needs to clearly sit above and dominate the body. I need to shrink the body's height or front radius so it stays lower than the head.

Adjusting body-head overlap slightly, I decide the join is visually fine since both pieces share the same pink tone. I'm refining proportions so the head stays bigger than the body for a chibi look, and updating the radius and path curves for body width, tail rise, and taper values.

Continuing the tail curve down through the hips, finishing with consistent thickness tapering values. Now I'm thinking about the tail fin membrane—a thin translucent pale pink extrusion running from the body's rear top to the tail tip with a ventral counterpart below, and working out how to rig it so it follows the nearest tail bone joint rather than needing its own skeleton.

I'll pass the chain as the bone reference for the membrane so the fin skin follows the tail smoothly. For simplicity, I'll just run a dorsal fin membrane from the rump toward the tail tip rather than trying to wrap it continuously from the head.

Defining the fin height curve...

Actually, thinking about ventral fin placement now - since the axolotl's tail sits on the ground, a lower fin would dip below the floor line, so I'm deciding to skip the ventral fin entirely and instead rely on a taller tail silhouette for visual weight.

For the dorsal fin, I want it running continuously from head to tail along the back's top edge, tapering in height and peaking near the tail, extending across most of the body's length rather than just the tail segment.

Still refining fin height function...

Now I'm thinking through the membrane painting approach, checking that negative lift values can bury edges, and planning how to sample points along the body path and resample the membrane edges by arc length to keep tangents consistent between the two surfaces.

For skinning, I'm weighing whether to specify a single bone or array for the membrane's bone weighting, since the fin spans multiple chain regions like hips and chest—I'm leaning toward skipping explicit bone assignment and letting the sweep's default weighting handle it since the rest pose is static anyway.

Now I'm turning to leg design: axolotl limbs are short and stubby, with thin four-fingered front legs and five-toed back legs splayed outward, and I'm sketching chibi-style stubby paws with the shoulder joints positioned along the body's sides for the rest pose extension.

Computing the distance between shoulder and hand target, I confirm the arm segments are long enough to reach with a bent elbow pointing outward-back-up. I'm now considering adding small finger capsules to the hand pad for extra detail.

Writing joint config...

Working out finger placement with four fingers fanned outward at small angles from forward, sized to taper near the floor, plus a flattened hand pad sphere positioned so its bottom edge touches the ground.

Now I'm thinking through the joint chain naming for each limb (shoulder/elbow/hand for front legs, hip/knee/foot for hind legs), parenting them to spine or pelvis joints, and placing hind foot targets splayed outward and backward from the hip root, checking the segment lengths add up correctly for the leg span.

I'm also working out limb tube radii and tapering so hand/foot tips sit flush with the ground pads without poking through, balancing target heights against the 2% tolerance, and figuring out where the elbow should sit between shoulder and hand given the outward bend hint.

Using two-bone IK math, I'm solving for the elbow position by finding the perpendicular offset from the shoulder-to-hand line toward the hint direction, landing on an elbow roughly at (0.07, 0.025, 0.016), which looks like a plausible outward-and-back bend.

For the hind leg, I run the same two-bone solve with root, target, and hint vectors to get a knee position around (0.07, 0.026, -0.06), which sits naturally to the side like a typical hind limb joint. I'll handle the actual numeric computation in code via the limb() function rather than by hand.

Now I'm thinking about toe counts and orientation — axolotls have 4 front toes and 5 hind toes, and I need to figure out the spread direction for each foot, with front toes angled forward-outward and hind toes likely pointing more backward-outward.

I'll add tiny dark spheres for nostrils stuck onto the dome, plus flat card-style blush decals on the cheeks using SVG shapes.

Adjusting alpha settings...

Sizing the eyes relative to head width, that looks proportionate. I'm positioning them at ±38° azimuth, 22° elevation on the dome.

That gives eye separation of 0.07, making the head width about 0.124, which fits the wide-set axolotl eye look. I'm now checking that the decal placement around the skull works correctly, and considering how the dome's lathe geometry handles UVs and normals — worried the flat bottom seam might create unwanted smooth shading across creases, though it's likely hidden anyway.

Still working out the geometry...

That orientation math works out, confirming the axis mapping. Thinking it might be simpler to avoid rotation complexity entirely by using a flattened sphere as a thin ellipsoid for the mouth roof and jaw, positioned just below the dome's open bottom to avoid any orientation issues altogether.

The jaw itself uses the bottom half of a sphere geometry, open at top, covered by a thin ellipsoid disc colored rose to act as the tongue or mouth floor, with a tiny vertical gap from the roof piece to prevent z-fighting while keeping both pieces slightly smaller in radius than the outer shell so they stay hidden inside.

Now I'm attaching the jaw to the hinge joint so it can rotate forward, adding a small rose ellipsoid tongue on the jaw floor, and considering whether the color contrast between the paler jaw and the pink dome naturally reads as a smile line along the seam, possibly skipping extra details like a lip torus or dimple to keep things simple.

I'm plotting the smile curve as a series of points along the seam that curve upward slightly toward the corners, following the dome's surface just above the jaw boundary, and giving it a thin dark reddish sweep with a small radius for a subtle mouth line. I'm noting that the upturned corners will sit slightly past where the jaw color boundary ends, which is a minor inconsistency I might need to address later.

For blush, I'm placing decal textures symmetrically at wide azimuth angles just above the seam, sized as small ellipses with a few accent lines, colored a deeper rose than the base skin tone. Then I'm shifting to designing the eyes as SVG shapes within a viewBox.

Placing tiny nostril dots, then working out gill positions along the back sides of the dome using azimuth and elevation angles, with a helper function to convert those angles into actual 3D points on the head.

Defining more gill path points...

Each stalk gets filaments spread around 6 angular positions, staggered between alternating sets, so the plume looks frilly from every side. I'm counting up the triangle budget per card including the bend segments and cross-doubling, trying to keep the total geometry manageable across all 180 filament positions.

Rather than varying card size continuously, I'll split each stalk into three groups with progressively smaller width and length toward the tip, calling the card generator separately for each group so the taper reads naturally while still sharing the same texture.

For the tip itself, I want to add a small cluster of spike-like cards angled more steeply along the stalk's direction, using the sweep frame's tangent as the flow direction so they orient toward growth direction rather than outward.

I should keep textures uncolored so they retain their own painted hues, and plan two filament color variants—a deep rose-red and a hot pink—to randomly vary between spikes for visual interest.

For finishing touches, I'll add a small bulb shape at the gill base to hide the sweep root, keeping the texture count reasonable (around 5-6): eye, blush, and the two filament variants, with freckles handled by skin paint rather than extra decals. I'll resist adding unnecessary accessories like sparkles or flowers and stick to what's essential for the chibi axolotl look.

I'm also double-checking the geometry so the gill filaments don't sink below the floor—working out the angle and length math to confirm the lowest point of each hanging filament stays just above y=0.

I'm also checking whether the gill stalks might collide with the arms, comparing their positions along the z-axis near the elbow and hand to make sure nothing overlaps awkwardly.

I'm recalculating the shoulder and hand placement so the arm clears the head's dome width, nudging the shoulder back to z=0 and the hand forward to z=.03, while making sure the body's rounded cap stays tucked behind the head's rear edge.

With the big head sitting over a short visible torso, the proportions read as a proper chibi shape. I'm also tracing the dorsal fin path along the back, checking that the curve's tangent and parameter points land smoothly from the tail tip up to the base of the head.

Now I'm working out the bone chain structure along the body path, splitting it into a "front" chain for the spine joints and a "back" chain for the tail joints, with hips as the pivot joint connecting them. I'm assigning roles to each joint—spine versus tail—and starting to set up the head joint parented to the last spine segment.

Using the chain's tip joint as the parent for each finger digit, with a simple two-point polyline path per finger so the joint aims toward the fingertip. I'm working out the vertical placement of hand and finger geometry so pads and fingertips sit flush with the ground plane.

Still writing finger sweep logic...

For texture decals, I'm weighing whether to add a few extra touches—dorsal speckles, freckles, or back stripe spots—to round out the 4-5 textures already planned, keeping within the 5-12 target range.

Adjusting the spot placement offset...

Now I'm scattering around 30 spots across the body surface sweep with a filter on normal direction and minimum distance so they form a dotted pattern over the body and tail, using a cropped circular texture for the alpha cutout. I'll skip adding spots to the fins for now, and briefly consider whether to add a decal for the eye using the skull part as a target.

I'm setting up helper functions and naming conventions for the rig, including limiting the flat color palette, handling left/right gill chain joint names based on sign, and writing a point-generation helper based on azimuth and elevation for the head.

Writing skin paint logic...

Writing fin membrane paint and eye decal SVG...

Finishing up the SVG with highlight circles for shine, then checking edge cases like transparency cutoff and gradient color parsing, and sketching a blush shape with a pink ellipse and lighter accent lines.

Now I'm defining a filament function that generates curved barb paths radiating outward with decreasing width, building the feather-like texture iteratively.

I'm double-checking the scaling math at size 128, making sure stroke widths and barb spans stay proportional, and settling on card dimensions around 0.038-0.05 for the feather. I'm also confirming the gradient needs userSpaceOnUse since objectBoundingBox fails on a zero-width line, and picking the stalk's gradient colors.

Now I'm starting the actual build script, importing the builder utilities and setting up the axolotl skeleton with joint positions like the hips.

Checking that the body sweep correctly derives radius per segment and orients the tube so its cross-section follows the frame's up direction along the spine/tail path.

I'm writing a keyframe interpolation helper that smoothsteps between control points, though I'm weighing whether linear or cosine easing would read more naturally than the plateau effect smoothstep introduces at each key.

Writing interpolation function...

Checking the hip radius against the path curvature looks consistent, so I'll move on to defining the head geometry—placing a sphere centered near the top with scaled radii to form a chibi-style skull, keeping segment counts low for a faceted but smooth-shaded low-poly look.

Adding jaw and mouth geometry...

Skipping teeth, then planning eye decals, blush, and nostrils. I consider adding a subtle eye-socket bulge for a bulging chibi-eye look but decide it's unnecessary complexity, then move to writing the gill creation function that computes positions along the head based on side, azimuth, elevation, and direction vectors.

Still writing gill curve points...

Still generating filament cards...

Now I'm sketching the gill bulb placement near the head root, then defining a set of gill descriptors with azimuth, elevation, direction vector, and length for each stalk (top, mid, and more).

I'm checking the resulting fan spread against body length to make sure it reads as a wide, axolotl-like gill cluster, then working through the direction-vector math for one of the elevation angles to verify the scaling factor lines up with the ellipsoid dimensions.

Now I'm defining the leg geometry function, setting root and target positions for front and back legs on each side based on offsets from center.

Building the chain from the polyline points with contact position, then sweeping it with tapered radii so the elbow corner gets smoothed into rounded limb skin. I'm working out which spine joint index to parent the front limbs to based on the spine's z-coordinates.

For the hand digits, I'm computing finger count and spread angles based on whether it's a front or back paw, deriving each finger's facing direction and rotating it around the vertical axis to fan out the digits from the base point.

Still writing finger chains...

Now I'm adding a pad sphere at the tip of each finger/toe chain, using a pale skin-toned color for consistency with the rest of the body rather than a distinct pad color.

For the fin membranes, I'm figuring out how to slice the body surface path to avoid the rounded cap regions at the tail end.

I should adjust the curve so the tip actually rises into a finlike shape, then move on to scattering textured spots across the body surface for coloring.

I'm working out the geometry for embedding small discs onto the curved sphere surface—tuples should handle the scale safely, but I need to account for surface curvature causing gaps at the disc edges, so lifting the center slightly actually makes edges float above the surface instead. I think sinking the center down a bit is the better fix.

Actually, I realize decals would be the cleaner solution here since they conform naturally to curved geometry, so I'm switching to using `b.decal` for each spot instead, with reduced segment counts to keep the triangle count manageable across all 34 spots.

Adding a pale belly and tail fin tip, then considering tiny mouth corner dimples but deciding to skip the extra crease detail along with eyelids and forehead sparkle since the jaw stays closed. Checking the module length is reasonable and reviewing the part helper signature for spheres with bone, position, scale, and color.

Now I'm working out decal placement parameters — size, position, direction, up vector, segment count, and lift — computing the decal direction from the hit normal and normalizing it into a proper vector, confirming that an explicit direction overrides the hit's default normal, and sizing the eyes with an aspect ratio in mind.

I'm defining a paint function for the jaw that blends pink tones based on surface normal direction, factoring in world-space normal values for lighting tint, and starting to think about how to shade the chest region next.

Belly and skin areas are handled with lighter tones. I'm tallying up the total mesh count across body, fins, head parts, decals, nostrils, gills, and limbs to make sure everything stays well under budget, landing around 130 meshes total, and considering whether small gill bud details near the cheeks would add enough visual interest to be worth it.

Now I'm double-checking some final implementation details—tail tip shading, skipping the eyelid, maybe adding subtle freckles via the skin paint—then verifying type correctness for the surface targeting calls, card frame arrays, and the rng seeding setup, while making sure the cards function call with multiple texture fills matches its expected signature.

Checking more wiring: gill chain bone weights follow the sweep frames, hind and front leg parenting connects properly to hip and shoulder joints, and limb functions return vector arrays usable as chain roots. I'm also confirming the digit chains build correctly from point arrays with proper tip-joint parenting before moving into the sweep call for the fin chain.

Writing sweep parameters...

Now I'm working out the smile curve's cheek corner position by computing the dome radius falloff, then comparing it against the jaw hemisphere's rim radius at the same angle to check whether the jaw edge sits inside or outside the smile endpoint.

Checking the jaw-to-dome seam, the jaw rim is slightly narrower than the dome, creating a clean lip step where the dome overhangs. I'm then confirming the smile line placement sits on that rim correctly, and moving to finalize the build function's export structure and joint parenting, verifying the head joint connects to the correct parent joint from the front piece.

Now I'm double-checking naming uniqueness across all the anatomical parts—tail segments, spine segments, gill pairs, and digits—making sure front fingers and hind toes use distinct naming patterns so nothing collides.

Gill chain roles need a "fan" option, which the allowed role list supports. I still need to add the nostril as a small embedded sphere stick, plus blush decals placed at specific azimuth positions on the dome, checking that decal normals default correctly without an explicit direction. I'm also setting up scattered spot decals across the body and tail with varying sizes.

Spot colors should read as a slightly deeper pink than the back, working as leucistic freckles, and I'm using thin ellipsoid spheres for the mouth floor and roof. For the arms, I'm sweeping the chain including the tip joint, which should work fine, and now I'm ready to write out the full assembly.
